# eSec — full documentation (llms-full.txt)

This file is a checked-in concatenation of eSec's documentation,
in the order listed below, so agents and tools can read the whole
corpus as one document. It is generated by hand from the sources —
when a source doc changes, update this file in the same commit.

Sources, in order:

- `docs/cra-reporting.md`
- `docs/cra-incident-reporting-runbook.md`
- `docs/cvd-intake.md`
- `docs/mbedtls-evaluation.md`
- `docs/mcp-hostile-protocol-hardening.md`

# === docs/cra-reporting.md ===

# CRA vulnerability reporting — triggers, channel, and templates

**Status:** operational runbook (2026-10-13), not legal counsel.
**Companion:** [`cra-incident-reporting-runbook.md`](cra-incident-reporting-runbook.md)
covers the incident workflow step by step; this page covers what
*triggers* a report, *who* files it, and the standing artifacts
(`security.txt`, SBOM, support period) that make filing possible
inside the clock. The org CVD policy in [`../SECURITY.md`](../SECURITY.md)
governs disclosure to reporters and the public.

## The clock

The CRA's reporting obligations have applied since **2026-09-11**:

| Deadline | What is filed |
|---|---|
| 24 hours | Early warning: an actively exploited vulnerability (or severe incident) has been confirmed, with initial details. |
| 72 hours | Fuller notification: impact, affected products and versions, mitigation status. |
| 14 days after a fix is available | Final report: root cause, complete impact, corrective measures. |

Full CRA obligations (beyond reporting) apply from **2027-12-11**.
Clocks run from triage confirmation, as defined in the companion
runbook — read that page for the workflow; this page assumes it.

## The trigger: what counts as "actively exploited"

The org's working trigger is a **CISA KEV listing**: a vulnerability
in the Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog is, by definition,
known to be actively exploited. This is the same signal the org
already tracks operationally — `embeddedos-stack`'s KEV gate
(`docs/kev-gate.md` in that repo) dispositions every KEV entry
against the stack, dated, so the trigger decision has a written
record before any incident starts.

In practice:

- A KEV entry matching a component in an org product starts the
  clock-assessment: triage confirms whether the shipped product is
  actually affected, and the runbook's classification applies.
- Credible exploitation evidence from any other source (researcher
  report, logs, honeypot) triggers the same assessment — KEV is the
  standing trigger, not the only one.
- A vulnerability with no exploitation evidence follows the normal
  CVD fix flow; it is recorded, but no CRA notification is due.

## The channel, and who files

- **Channel:** the ENISA single reporting platform — one submission
  reaches ENISA and the relevant national CSIRTs; there is no
  separate per-country filing for the early warning.
- **Who files:** the maintainer holding the **product security
  lead** role for the affected product (with the named deputy from
  the companion runbook's readiness list as fallback). Roles, not
  personal names, are recorded here — the current role-holders live
  in the private advisory template.
- The filer files even when fields are "unknown, under assessment";
  a late complete report is a missed deadline, an early incomplete
  one is the process working.

## Standing artifact: `security.txt` (RFC 9116)

Every org product ships a `security.txt` so a reporter can find the
intake before an incident exists. Template (this repo's own live
copy is [`../.well-known/security.txt`](../.well-known/security.txt)):

```text
Contact: https://github.com/embeddedos-org/<repo>/security/advisories/new
Expires: <one year from issue, ISO 8601 UTC>
Preferred-Languages: en
Policy: https://github.com/embeddedos-org/<repo>/blob/master/SECURITY.md
```

Expiry discipline is the operational point: an expired `Expires:`
field silently breaks the reporting path, so the date is reviewed
whenever the file is touched and at least yearly. Fields follow
RFC 9116; no field a product cannot honour may be listed.

## Supporting regime (design inputs)

Two CRA duties shape engineering before any incident:

- **SBOM.** Products maintain a software bill of materials
  (CycloneDX or SPDX). The SBOM is what turns "is the KEV-listed
  component in our product?" from an archaeology project into a
  lookup that fits inside the 24-hour clock.
- **Update support.** Products are designed for a support period of
  at least **five years**: update infrastructure, signing keys, and
  build reproducibility must be provisioned for that horizon, not
  for the launch quarter.

Both are design inputs to new products, reviewed like any other
requirement — not paperwork reconstructed after an incident.

## Worked timeline — MCP gateway auth-bypass class (hypothetical)

A worked example, end to end, for the failure shape this org's
agent fabric is most exposed to: an MCP gateway endpoint that
accepts an asserted identity without proof — the spoofing class
(CWE-290) behind the LiteLLM MCP auth-bypass vulnerability
(CVE-2026-59822, KEV-listed September 2026, where a fabricated
Bearer token opened an authenticated MCP session). **This is a
hypothetical exercise against that pattern, not a report of an
incident in any EmbeddedOS product.** Its point is to prove the
clock above is achievable with the artifacts this repo maintains.

Scenario: a future EmbeddedOS product ships with an MCP gateway
component. A researcher reports — via the `security.txt`
channel — that the gateway's session endpoint accepts a
placeholder credential and opens a session, and demonstrates
read access to a tool that should require authentication.
Telemetry suggests the endpoint is reachable in deployed units.

| Clock | Action | Artifact |
|---|---|---|
| T+0 h | Report received via the RFC 9116 contact; acknowledged to the reporter; incident opened | `security.txt` channel (above) |
| T+2 h | Triage confirms the claim against the product build; gateway sessions revoked, affected tool disabled by configuration; credentials the gateway held are rotated | SBOM lookup answers "which products/versions ship the gateway" inside this window — that is what the SBOM duty above is for |
| T+24 h | **Early warning** filed to the competent CSIRT / single reporting platform: vulnerability identified, products affected, exploitation suspected (a public proof exists) | CRA Art. 14 early warning — the 24-hour duty in "The clock" |
| T+72 h | **Notification** filed with the fuller assessment: root cause (asserted identity accepted without verification), exposure window, mitigations shipped | CRA Art. 14 notification |
| T+14 d | **Final report**: fix released (sessions require verified credentials; placeholder/asserted-only tokens are refused and logged), update pushed through the product's normal signed-update path, residual-risk note | CRA Art. 14 final report |

Two lessons the exercise is designed to teach before it is real:

- The 24-hour filing is only possible because the SBOM and the
  `security.txt` channel already exist. Both are maintained in
  quiet times (the `security.txt` expiry is CI-enforced in this
  repo) or they do not exist at all.
- The fix pattern is the same one the org applies to tensor
  descriptors and update images: an identity claim is verified,
  never trusted — and the regression test is a request with a
  fabricated credential expecting refusal.

## What this page is not

Legal advice. The CRA text and ENISA guidance are authoritative;
when they change, this page and the companion runbook follow.

# === docs/cra-incident-reporting-runbook.md ===

# CRA incident-reporting runbook (EU Cyber Resilience Act)

**Status:** Maintainer runbook. **Date:** 2026-10-05
**Companion docs:** `docs/cvd-intake.md` (reporter-facing intake),
`SECURITY.md` (org CVD policy).

> **Urgency:** the CRA's vulnerability-reporting obligations have applied
> since **11 September 2026**. Fines reach €15M or 2.5% of worldwide
> turnover. This runbook maps those obligations onto the org's existing
> coordinated vulnerability disclosure (CVD) process.

## 1. The three CRA deadlines

All clocks start when the org **becomes aware** of the incident — i.e.
when a private security advisory (or credible report) lands in eSec and
triage confirms it is real. "Becoming aware" is the triage-confirmation
timestamp, not the report-arrival timestamp; record both.

| Deadline | What | To whom |
|---|---|---|
| **24 hours** | Early notification: the fact of an actively exploited vulnerability or a severe incident, with initial details | ENISA via the single reporting platform, **and** the CSIRT of the Member State(s) where affected products are on the market |
| **72 hours** | Severe-incident notification: fuller details — impact, affected products/versions, mitigation status | Same channels |
| **14 days** | Final report: root cause, complete impact assessment, corrective measures taken | Same channels |

A **severe incident** = one that affects the availability, authenticity,
integrity, or confidentiality of data/services, or that has cross-border
impact. When in doubt, treat it as severe — over-reporting within the
deadlines is safe; missing a deadline is not.

## 2. Severity classification (triage → CRA track)

Triage in the private advisory first, using the existing
`docs/cvd-intake.md` fields, then classify:

- **Actively exploited** (evidence of exploitation in the wild, not just a
  PoC) → the 24h clock applies. Confirm exploitation evidence before
  filing, but do not wait for perfect certainty — file the early
  notification and update it.
- **Severe incident** (per the definition above) → 72h notification + 14d
  final report.
- **Non-severe vulnerability** (no active exploitation, no severe
  impact) → no CRA notification duty, but the normal CVD fix flow still
  applies, and the vulnerability goes into the org's records for the
  technical documentation file.

Record the classification decision and its rationale in the advisory's
triage notes — the market-surveillance authority may ask why a track was
chosen.

## 3. What the disclosure must contain

Map the ENISA/CSIRT fields onto the advisory sections:

| CRA field | Source in our process |
|---|---|
| Affected product(s) and versions | Intake: "Affected component" (repo, version/commit, board/target) |
| Nature of the vulnerability / incident | Intake: "Description" + "Reproduction" |
| Severity and impact | Intake: "Impact" (attacker capability, prerequisites, severity estimate) |
| Whether exploitation is observed | Triage: exploitation evidence (logs, reports, honeypot hits) |
| Mitigation / corrective measures | Triage: "Fix PR / commit", plus user-facing mitigations |
| Number of affected users/products (if known) | Estimate; "unknown, under assessment" is acceptable at 24h |

## 4. Runbook: when triage confirms a real report

1. **Timestamp it.** Record report-arrival and triage-confirmation times
   in the advisory. The 24h/72h clocks run from confirmation.
2. **Classify** (see §2) and write the rationale into triage notes.
3. **Draft the 24h early notification** from the intake fields — even if
   some are "unknown". File it; do not wait for the fix.
4. **Start the fix in parallel** (private branch, security advisory
   workflow). The 72h notification must describe mitigation status, so
   the fix timeline matters.
5. **72h notification:** update with impact assessment, affected
   versions, and mitigation status.
6. **14d final report:** root cause, complete impact, corrective measures,
   and confirmation the fix is shipped.
7. **Close the loop:** link the ENISA/CSIRT case references back into the
   advisory; keep the advisory private until coordinated disclosure.

## 5. Standing readiness (do this before an incident)

- [ ] One maintainer owns the ENISA single-reporting-platform account and
  the CSIRT contact list; a deputy is named. (Names live in the private
  advisory template, not in this public doc.)
- [ ] The intake template's "Triage notes" already has fields for the two
  timestamps and the CRA classification — keep them.
- [ ] SBOM generation (`ebuild sbom`, where available) is the fastest way
  to answer "which products/versions are affected" — keep it working.
- [ ] Review this runbook after every incident (add a "lessons" section to
  the advisory) and at least yearly.

## 6. What this runbook is not

Legal advice. The CRA text and ENISA guidance are authoritative; when
they change, this runbook follows. The org's CVD policy (`SECURITY.md`)
governs disclosure to reporters and the public; this runbook governs
disclosure to authorities.

# === docs/cvd-intake.md ===

# Vulnerability report intake

Copy this template into a
[private security advisory](https://github.com/embeddedos-org/eSec/security/advisories/new).
Fill in every section you can; "unknown" is an acceptable answer, a blank
section is not — it tells triage what still needs discovery.

## Affected component

- Repository:
- Version / commit:
- Board / target (if firmware):
- Configuration (build type, feature flags):

## Description

What is wrong, in one paragraph. Then the details: which file and function,
what the code does, and why that is a vulnerability rather than a bug.

## Reproduction

Steps, commands, or a minimal proof of concept. For a firmware issue, note
the hardware or simulator (EoSim) it was reproduced on.

## Impact

- What can an attacker achieve? (code execution, privilege escalation,
  information disclosure, denial of service, secure-boot bypass, …)
- What must the attacker already have? (physical access, a signed package,
  network adjacency, …)
- Your severity estimate and why:

## Suggested fix

Optional, but welcome — especially a pointer to how a comparable project
fixed the same class of issue.

## Reporter

- Name / handle (for credit in the advisory):
- Contact for follow-up questions:
- Disclosure preference: [ ] coordinated disclosure after fix
  [ ] full disclosure on a date: ____
  [ ] keep my name out of the public advisory

## Triage notes (maintainers only)

- Reproduced: [ ] yes [ ] no — notes:
- Severity:
- Fix PR / commit:
- CVE requested: [ ] yes [ ] no — ID:
- Advisory published:

# === docs/mbedtls-evaluation.md ===

# Mbed TLS evaluation for issue #5 milestone 1

**Repo:** `embeddedos-org/eSec` ·
**Decision of record:**
[ADR-012 — cryptographic provider selection](https://github.com/embeddedos-org/eos/blob/master/docs/adr/ADR-012-cryptographic-provider-selection.md)
(Proposed) ·
**Tracker:** [issue #5](https://github.com/embeddedos-org/eSec/issues/5)
("merge `eos/services/{security,crypto}` into eSec, 3 milestones")

This evaluation feeds **milestone 1** of issue #5: land ADR-012 — the Mbed TLS swap
for hand-rolled AES/SHA/RSA/ECC — so the `EOS_ALLOW_STUB_CRYPTO` stub gate
disappears with real verification. **No code moves in this document and none is
proposed to move here.** The merge decision remains with the issue tracker; this
document only records what the swap costs, what it buys, and what would change.

---

## 1. Current inventory: what `eos` ships today

Verified 2026-10-11 via the GitHub API against `embeddedos-org/eos`
(`GET /repos/embeddedos-org/eos/contents/services/crypto`, walking
`include/` and `src/` recursively). The eSec README's "16 source files (10 `.c`,
6 internal headers)" holds once the two *public* headers are counted separately:
**10 `.c` files, 6 internal headers, 2 public headers** (18 files, plus
`CMakeLists.txt`).

| File | Size | What it is |
|---|---|---|
| `src/aes.c` | ~9.4 KB | Hand-written AES (ECB/CBC-era design) |
| `src/sha256.c` | ~5.1 KB | Hand-written SHA-256 |
| `src/ed25519_fe.c` / `_ge.c` / `_sc.c` | ~73.5 KB | Hand-written Curve25519 field arithmetic |
| `src/ed25519_sha512.c`, `src/sha512.h` | ~11.6 KB | Hand-written SHA-512 |
| `src/ed25519_sign.c` / `_verify.c` | ~10.2 KB | Hand-written Ed25519 sign/verify |
| `src/precomp_data.h` | **~97.8 KB** | Precomputed Ed25519 tables (ROM pressure) |
| `src/fe.h`, `src/ge.h`, `src/sc.h`, `src/fixedint.h` | ~5.4 KB | Internal headers |
| `src/rsa_ecc_sha512.c` | ~9.9 KB | **RSA/ECDSA stubs — fail closed** |
| `src/crc.c` | ~2.1 KB | CRC-32 (not cryptographic; out of scope) |
| `include/eos/crypto.h` | ~4.3 KB | Public API |
| `include/ed25519.h` | ~1.6 KB | Public Ed25519 API |

The companion `services/security/` (`include/eos/security.h`, `src/security.c`)
holds the security framework: `eos_secureboot_verify_image()` calls
`eos_rsa_verify_sha256()`.

**What the code actually covers — and what it does not:**

- **Functional (NIST-vector passing):** AES, SHA-256, SHA-512, Ed25519 sign.
  Ed25519 *verification* is a known gap: per ADR-012 §5, the RFC 8032 §7.1
  vectors for verification **fail**, and they are the acceptance test for this
  work. A hand-written Ed25519 verify that fails standard vectors is exactly the
  code an attacker scrutinises first.
- **Stubs that refuse to run:** `eos_rsa_sign/verify_sha256`,
  `eos_ecc_sign/verify`, `eos_ecdsa_*` — `rsa_ecc_sha512.c` implements none of
  PKCS#1, PSS, or ECDSA. Without `EOS_ALLOW_STUB_CRYPTO` they print to stderr
  and return `-1`. The old versions were forgeable (the verify stub once
  accepted any 64-byte "signature"), and a real exploit path existed: secure
  boot consumed `eos_rsa_verify_sha256()`. Fail-closed is the right posture,
  but it means **secure boot with RSA currently cannot verify at all in a
  production build** — the stub *is* the feature.
- **Absent entirely:** TLS (any version), X.509 parsing/generation/verification,
  certificate chains, AEAD modes (GCM, CCM, ChaCha20-Poly1305), KDFs
  (PBKDF2/HKDF), DRBG, hardware-acceleration hooks. There is no story for a
  device that must terminate TLS to an OEM cloud or join a mutually-authenticated
  mesh.
- **Second copy:** `eBoot/core/` carries its own hand-rolled SHA-512 and an
  Ed25519 verify (ADR-012 context) — the same low-order-key bypass class existed
  in both copies, which is precisely the duplication the eSec README warns
  about.

## 2. Mbed TLS 3.x capability map

Mbed TLS 3.x is the current stable line; **3.6.4** is the recommended LTS
release as of October 2026 (the 4.0 line is in beta and explicitly not
production-ready). Verified against the Mbed-TLS releases page and Trusted
Firmware release notes.

- **TLS:** full TLS 1.3 (client and server, ephemeral key establishment,
  pre-shared keys, client authentication, server-side TLS 1.2/1.3 version
  negotiation, DTLS) alongside TLS 1.2. FFDH key exchange in TLS 1.3.
- **X.509:** parse, verify, generate; certificate chains, CSR parsing and
  generation, hostname verification, `cert_write` (PEM and DER), extended key
  usage.
- **PSA Crypto API:** Mbed TLS 3.x ships the PSA Crypto reference
  implementation and passes the PSA compliance suite. Since 3.1, essentially
  all TLS/X.509/PK operations run *through* PSA under the hood
  (`MBEDTLS_USE_PSA_CRYPTO` is effectively the only mode now). This is the
  interface that matters: silicon vendors map their crypto accelerators to the
  PSA driver interface, so the same call reaches software on one part and a
  crypto co-processor on another.
- **Footprint controls for MCUs:** `p256-m` (compact SECP256R1 via PSA —
  much smaller code and RAM than the classic ECP), `MBEDTLS_AES_ONLY_128_BIT_KEY_LENGTH`,
  ability to compile out AES/bignum/EC modules when PSA drivers provide them,
  PSA-client-only builds that offload everything to an external server.
- **Algorithmic breadth:** SHA-3, PBKDF2-HMAC/CMAC, HKDF, LMS/LM-OTS
  (post-quantum *verification* for firmware images), ChaCha20-Poly1305,
  CCM/GCM.
- **Maintenance:** a published security-advisory process with CVE-level
  disclosures and LTS backports — i.e. when a primitive breaks, there is a
  versioned upstream fix to pull instead of a hand-written line to patch.

## 3. Gap analysis: what `eos` lacks that Mbed TLS provides

| Need | `eos` today | Mbed TLS 3.x |
|---|---|---|
| TLS (client/server, 1.2/1.3) | Nothing | Complete |
| X.509 chain verification, cert issuance | Nothing | Complete |
| RSA/ECDSA verification that *works* | Fail-closed stubs | Production crypto |
| Ed25519 verification matching RFC 8032 | Hand-written, vectors fail | Verified implementation |
| AEAD (GCM/CCM/ChaCha20-Poly1305) | Nothing | Complete |
| KDFs (HKDF/PBKDF2) | Nothing | Complete |
| Hardware accelerator mapping | None | PSA driver interface |
| Advisory feed for discovered breaks | None (silent) | Published advisories + LTS backports |
| Secure boot end-to-end | Experimental, no real trust anchor shipped | Working verify + LMS for image signing |

The shape of the gap is what matters: it is not that `eos` has slow crypto —
it is that `eos` has **no verifiable asymmetric crypto and no transport
security at all**, while continuing to ship a secure-boot feature that depends
on both. Every new protocol the platform adds (OTA, device identity,
attestation) would otherwise re-invent these under the hand-rolled constraint.

## 4. Swap criteria for ADR-012

ADR-012 is **Proposed**, and names its own acceptance criteria. This evaluation
recommends holding it there until each is met — they are blocking
prerequisites, not follow-ups:

1. **Footprint budget for MCU targets.** Flash and RAM deltas must be measured
   on the smallest §21 Nano target in *both* configurations: the eBoot
   verify-only subset (SHA-512 + Ed25519 verify, everything else compiled out)
   and the full `eos` configuration. The 97.8 KB of precomputed Ed25519 tables
   leaves the tree; the Mbed TLS replacement's tables are the number to
   compare against, not a slogan.
2. **PSA alignment.** `eos/services/crypto/include/eos/crypto.h` stays as the
   EoS-facing API and becomes a thin shim over the PSA Crypto API, not over
   legacy `mbedtls_*` calls. This is what preserves the hardware-accelerator
   path: a future board's crypto co-processor plugs in as a PSA driver, and no
   call site changes.
3. **CRA SBOM implications.** A first third-party dependency in `eos` changes
   the compliance story: exact upstream version pinned, `NOTICE` attribution
   (Mbed TLS is Apache-2.0; ADR-012 flags re-verifying at import), SBOM entry
   per the EU Cyber Resilience Act obligations, and the project's security
   advisories wired into the intake process already standing up in eSec
   (`docs/cvd-intake.md`, `.well-known/security.txt`). A reviewed provider is
   only reviewed if it is *identifiable, versioned, and tracked* — ADR-012's
   provenance argument from the PR #57 rejection applies to the dependency
   itself.
4. **Conformance vectors in CI, deletion not coexistence.** Each adopted
   primitive lands with published vectors (FIPS 180-4, FIPS-197, RFC 8032
   §7.1) executing in the test suite; the hand-written file is deleted in the
   same commit its PSA replacement lands. CRC-32 stays (not a primitive).

Alternatives considered by ADR-012 stand: BearSSL (smaller, no PSA mapping —
forfeits the accelerator argument), libsodium verify-only (would mean two
providers), wolfSSL (GPLv2-or-commercial — incompatible with the MIT runtime),
and repairing the hand-rolled code (rejected by ADR-011 item 2).

## 5. Threat-model note: the Oct-2026 perimeter zero-day density

The perimeter-appliance CVE cluster of autumn 2026 is the strongest argument
for a fail-closed, maintained crypto substrate:

- **Cisco CVE-2026-76504** — added to the CISA Known Exploited Vulnerabilities
  catalog on 2026-09-30.
- **SonicWall CVE-2026-83548** — KEV-listed in early September; then
  **CVE-2026-102255** (CVSS 10.0, pre-authentication SSRF in the SMA1000
  Work Place interface, disclosed 2026-10-07) — the *third* pre-auth SSRF in
  the same interface in 2026, not yet KEV-listed but with exploitation
  attempts observed within 48 hours of disclosure.
- **FortiMail CVE-2026-104286** — KEV-listed 2026-10-01.

The pattern is not "four vendors had a bad month." It is that the appliances
sitting at trust boundaries — the exact network position EoS targets will
increasingly occupy in industrial and edge roles — are being probed with
pre-authentication remote flaws at a cadence measured in weeks, and the same
interface keeps yielding new zero-days after patching.

The lesson for this platform is fail-closed at every layer:

- An MCU target cannot absorb a weekly hotfix cadence. Its defence is (a)
  minimise the attack surface of the trusted code, and (b) make every
  unverifiable primitive **refuse** — which `eos` already does with
  `EOS_ALLOW_STUB_CRYPTO`, but only by leaving the feature absent.
- A maintained upstream with a published advisory feed (Mbed TLS's security
  advisories + LTS backports) is the only realistic way a small platform team
  matches the fix velocity of the threat. Hand-rolled crypto gets neither a
  fuzzing community nor a backport — when it breaks, it breaks silently.
- Until the swap lands, the honest status is the one ADR-011 requires:
  `EOS_SIG_ED25519` is **non-functional**, and package-signature verification
  stays Experimental. Inflating either is how the perimeter appliances in the
  CVE list got their "secure" labels.

## 6. Recommendation and milestone 1 changes

**Recommendation:** adopt Mbed TLS 3.6.x LTS via the PSA Crypto API as the
cryptographic provider for `eos`, per ADR-012 — contingent on the four swap
criteria in §4, with the footprint measurement as the blocking prerequisite.
The alternatives were weighed in ADR-012 and the weighting stands; the CVE
cluster in §5 only hardens the maintenance argument.

**What milestone 1 changes in `eos` (all in-tree, none of it in this repo):**

1. `services/crypto/src/aes.c` and `src/sha256.c` deleted; `eos/crypto.h`
   re-implemented as a thin PSA shim.
2. Real RSA/ECDSA/Ed25519 via Mbed TLS; `rsa_ecc_sha512.c` and the
   fail-closed stubs deleted; `EOS_ALLOW_STUB_CRYPTO` retired — nothing that
   pretends to verify remains.
3. RFC 8032 §7.1 verification vectors (currently failing) pass in CI, along
   with FIPS 180-4 and FIPS-197 vectors per primitive.
4. eBoot links the verify-only Mbed TLS configuration (SHA-512 + Ed25519
   verify; no signing, no TLS, no AEAD in the boot chain), deleting its
   hand-rolled SHA-512 and Ed25519 verify.
5. SBOM + `NOTICE` entries for the pinned Mbed TLS version land with the
   import; ADR-012 moves Proposed → Accepted.

Issue #5 stays open: milestones 2 (API stabilisation) and 3 (the `git subtree
split`, gated on Aswin's decision per §11) are untouched by this document.

# === docs/mcp-hostile-protocol-hardening.md ===

# MCP hostile-protocol hardening

Date: 2026-10-07.

Posture: treat the **Model Context Protocol itself as hostile-by-default** —
not just the server implementations. Two converging disclosures this week
forced this stance:

- **ClawSecure AI Agent Threat Report Vol 1** (Sept 24, reported Oct 6):
  cracked MCP integrations (Linear, Notion, Dropbox Dash) — the report's
  central finding is that "the gap sits in the MCP protocol itself," not only
  in individual servers.
- **Mohiuddin analysis**: the MCP specification carries **no normative
  security requirements** — security is currently conventional, not mandated.

In other words: even a spec-conformant MCP deployment cannot be assumed safe.

## Hardening controls

1. **Allowlisted servers.** Only explicitly listed MCP servers may be
   attached to agents. Discovery-on-the-network is off by default.
2. **Pinned server versions.** Pin exact versions; upgrades are a deliberate
   review event, not `latest`.
3. **Credential isolation.** Agents' credentials are never handed to MCP
   servers; servers authenticate with their own scoped tokens. A compromised
   server must not become a launchpad into other systems (Oct-6 chain-of-trust
   analysis: one compromised agent = launchpad across every agent that trusts
   it).
4. **Upstream-response redaction.** Error messages, tool outputs, and
   response envelopes are scrubbed of secrets/PII before they cross trust
   boundaries — redaction is a transport requirement, not a logging
   afterthought. (See also the Oct-6 report: a US federal MCP server logged
   veterans' SSNs in *unredacted* error responses, unpatched 6 weeks
   post-disclosure.)
5. **No implicit intra-network trust.** Agents and servers inside the same
   network do not trust each other by default; every call re-authenticates.
6. **Tool-registration command allowlists.** Any tool registration that can
   cause command execution declares the exact commands/paths allowed; a
   config-supplied command is untrusted input, never interpolated into a
   shell string. (CVE-2026-105697 below is the CVSS 9.9 proof this control
   is load-bearing.)

## Threat taxonomy: the six MCP attack classes

The Agentics' *Enterprise MCP Guide 2026* (Oct 5) names six attack
classes — with 68 MCP server CVEs disclosed in one month as the
backdrop. Each maps to an existing control above; the guide is the
external validation of this posture.

| # | Attack class | What it is | eSec control |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | **Tool poisoning** | A tool's description is altered to smuggle malicious instructions into the agent's context | Control 1 (allowlisted servers) + pinned descriptions at registration |
| 2 | **Schema poisoning** | The declared parameter schema is widened beyond what the tool honestly accepts | Boundary schema validation — descriptors are validated, never trusted |
| 3 | **Tool shadowing** | A lower-privilege tool overrides a higher-privilege tool's identity | Privilege-scoped registration: no shadowing across trust levels; collisions fail closed |
| 4 | **Command injection** | Tool arguments become shell commands | Control 6 (command allowlists) — CVE-2026-105697 is the CVSS 9.9 proof |
| 5 | **Shadow servers** | Rogue servers the agent discovers and trusts | Control 1 + Control 5 (no implicit intra-network trust; every call re-authenticates) |
| 6 | **Context oversharing** | Tools receive more context than they need | Control 3 (credential isolation) + Control 4 (upstream redaction) |

The guide's control set — per-agent allowlists, identity binding,
centralized MCP gateways, human approval for destructive actions —
is the day-one posture the agent-fabric gateway evaluation
(`embeddedos-org/EoSim` `docs/mcp-gateway-eval.md`) now requires.

## Evidence links

- unite.ai — researcher disclosure on the MCP protocol gap.
- techtimes (Oct 6) — 5 US federal MCP servers unpatched 6 weeks post-disclosure.
- einpresswire — ClawSecure AI Agent Threat Report Vol 1.
- CVE-2026-105697 (CVSS 9.9, Oct 5) — Langflow MCP server config executed
  the user-typed `command` via `bash -c` with no allowlist: config-file
  command execution. Patch 1.10.3. Control 6 is the mitigation.
- CVE-2026-104120 (Oct 2) — `mcp-server-fetch` <= 2026.6.4 SSRF via
  `fetch_url`, publicly disclosed exploit. Fetch-style tools are network
  egress: allowlisted destinations only.

## Trust-track input: Logic Fruit L-Nex (2026-10-06)

L-Nex is an FPGA-based OCP DC-SCM 2.x BMC running OpenBMC, announced with
a hardware root of trust (secure + measured boot, attestation,
NIST SP 800-193) and "a path to post-quantum cryptography without
replacing the management architecture." Three angles for the eBoot/eSec
trust tracks:

1. **NIST SP 800-193 as the compliance anchor.** Protection, detection,
   and recovery for firmware resiliency -- the same triad the KEV/CRA
   docs already track. L-Nex shipping it in a BMC is the precedent for
   requiring it in our boot design docs.
2. **PQC crypto-agility without re-spin.** L-Nex's post-quantum path
   argues for *measured-boot crypto agility* in eBoot: the boot chain
   must be able to swap signature algorithms without a hardware
   re-spin. The #162 envelope's algorithm agility is the software side
   of this.
3. **Measured boot + attestation as table stakes.** A BMC shipping
   attestation in 2026 means our boot chain's attestation story is not
   a differentiator -- it is the entry ticket.

## Standing KEV/CRA input

The monthly dev.to "Open-Source Device CVEs: What to Patch by Vertical"
series is the standing human-readable layer over the KEV feed for
bootloader-class upstreams (Mbed TLS, U-Boot, TF-A) and is tracked as part of
the org's CRA-readiness posture.

## Appendix: worked examples (October 2026)

Timestamped, CVE-numbered proof the taxonomy above is live — not theoretical.

**Langflow CVE-2026-105697 (CVSS 9.9, disclosed Oct 5).** OS command
injection in MCP server handling: the stdio transport launched a
user-supplied `command`/`args` pair via `bash -c` with no allowlist on the
executable and no validation of the arguments. Public proof-of-concept;
fixed in 1.10.3. The flaw was not in Langflow's business logic but in its
*protocol handling* — which is why the command-injection control has to
live at the trust boundary (allowlisted executables, declared at
registration), not inside each tool. This is the class the eIPC
tool-registration allowlist and the eVera tool-use policy exist for.

**ClawSecure AI Agent Threat Report Vol 1 (Sept 24).** Three clean,
production MCP implementations — Linear, Notion, Dropbox Dash — cracked
with the same attack class. Three independent codebases, three vendors,
one flaw shape: when the same class lands in three clean implementations,
the defect is in the protocol's missing security requirements, not in any
one implementation. That is the entire reason a hostile-protocol hardening
document has to exist: the MCP spec's lack of normative security
requirements pushes the security burden onto every implementer, and most
implementers will not carry it.

## Appendix: the October 2026 OAuth/session cluster (2026-10-20)

Three advisories in nine days, one shared shape — **trust placed in
counterparty-supplied metadata, and fallbacks that authenticate
nobody**:

- **CVE-2026-104850 / GHSA-6qxp-vccf-f47h** (high, 2026-10-06) —
  MCP TypeScript SDK: an OAuth client could be steered to send
  credentials to an authorization server chosen by the MCP server
  (issuer confusion). Affected `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk`
  >= 1.12.0 < 1.31.0 and `@modelcontextprotocol/client`
  >= 2.0.0 < 2.2.0; fixed in 1.31.0 / 2.2.0.
- **CVE-2026-59822 / GHSA-7488-6r32-c95q** (2026-10-13) —
  LiteLLM's MCP Streamable HTTP endpoint allowed unauthenticated
  session establishment through an OAuth2-passthrough fallback: a
  fabricated `Authorization` header was treated as authenticated.
  Fixed in LiteLLM 1.84.0.
- **CVE-2026-59951 / GHSA-84m7-p3x7-pcfv** (medium, 2026-10-15) —
  MCP Python SDK: unbounded session accumulation in the
  StreamableHTTP transport allows resource exhaustion.

Two controls follow directly and are adopted here as additions to
the list above:

7. **Authorization-server identity is pinned, never discovered from
   the counterparty.** A server may not choose, redirect, or
   substitute the issuer a client authenticates against
   (CVE-2026-104850). This is Control 5 applied to identity
   metadata: the issuer is configuration, not protocol data.
8. **Authentication has no fallback path, and sessions are a
   bounded resource.** A failed or absent credential is terminal —
   never a passthrough to an authenticated session
   (CVE-2026-59822) — and any stateful transport caps concurrent
   sessions and expires idle ones (CVE-2026-59951). An
   unauthenticated peer must not be able to allocate unbounded
   server state.

**Org exposure, measured 2026-10-20 (code search, not assumed):**
no repository in the org uses `@modelcontextprotocol/sdk`
(zero hits org-wide), and the org's MCP servers (EoSim, eFlow,
eosllm) are stdio transports with no OAuth flow — the
issuer-confusion and passthrough classes do not reach them as
built. The one dependency thread, eVera's LiteLLM, was assessed
the same day: `pyproject.toml` floors it at `>= 1.40` and
`requirements.txt` at `>= 1.0.0` (floors, not pins — nothing
holds it below the 1.84.0 fix), `vera.spec` carries no version
pin, and no code serves LiteLLM's proxy or MCP endpoint.
CVE-2026-59822 is therefore **assessed, not applicable** to
eVera as built; it becomes applicable the day any org component
exposes a LiteLLM proxy endpoint, which is why the control
belongs here rather than in a per-repo note.

The cluster is also the worked example for the agent fabric's
gateway evaluation: a gateway is exactly where counterparty
metadata concentrates, so the gateway inherits Controls 7–8 as
acceptance criteria, alongside the eNet bridge trial's "no
unauthenticated fallback path" exit check.
